en.html:
...A little rain had started, it seemed.

Perhaps because the walls were thin, even that light rain made itself heard very clearly.

Since work on the bridge began, I had been staying at Hikari's house. Outskirts or not, this was still Kamakura. Coming from the chief's house every day would have been no trouble. Still, I had my reasons for staying here.

For my host, I brought food and other necessities in return. In these times, and for a child living alone, cash was not necessarily the most useful form of thank-you. This seemed better.

en.html:
Once, I had asked whether she would like to come and live with me. Not even a little hesitation in the answer.

Hikari shook her head. She would wait here for her mother to return.

After that, I did not bring it up again.

Her mother had disappeared without warning, she said. The chance of her coming back was almost nothing—or so I thought. Dead, of course she would not return. But even alive, probably not.

That did not mean I should say all this and persuade Hikari to agree with me. What good would that do her? None that I could see. So I kept my mouth closed.

She appeared to be alone. But for her, the family was still there. As long as she believed it, still there. On the strength of my own judgment, I had no right to take that away.

Being kind did not give me permission to march across the distance between us. We were strangers; respecting that distance was what I could do for her. Leave her sanctuary alone.

From the other side of that distance, Hikari was now watching me. What was in those eyes, I could not quite read.

ja.html:
一度、一緒に暮らさないかと持ち掛けてみた。
　その返答は迷いなく。

　ここで母の帰りを待つからと、光は首を横に振った。
　
　以来、その話はしていない。

　前触れもなく姿を消したという母親が戻る見込みは
皆無に近い――そう思う。
　死んでいれば当然、生きていてもだ。

　しかし、そこまで口にして光を説き伏せるべきとは
思われなかった。それは全く彼女にとって良い事では
ないと思えた。
　だから俺は口を噤んだ。

　彼女は独りきりに見える。
　だが家族は<ruby>まだいる<rt>・・・・</rt></ruby>のだ――彼女がそう信じる限り。
俺の独断でそれを取り上げて良い筈はない。

　俺にできる親切とは、他人同士の距離を踏み越える
事ではなく守る事であった。彼女の聖域を侵さぬよう。
　その距離から今、光は俺に不分明な眼差しを注いで
いる。

en.html:
Such a small question. No difficulty understanding what she meant, though: my going to the refugees and trying to rebuild the bridge with them.

Had she watched the whole thing? Or had she understood without needing to see, with some strange sense that grown-ups did not possess? Somehow she knew I was trying.

Kageaki"Harmony is to be valued."
Hikari"Harmy?"
Kageaki"Harmony."
Hikari"Harmony."
Kageaki"Is to be valued."
Hikari"Is to be val-yood."
Kageaki"Yes."
Hikari"...What's that?"
Kageaki"Something a great person said long ago. Getting along with each other is important—that is what he was saying."
Kageaki"If we only go on fighting, nothing gets done. If we help each other instead, anything can be done... that is why."
Hikari"Anything?"
Kageaki"Yes. Growing food, building houses..."
Hikari"A zoo also?"
Kageaki"That can be done."
Hikari"A movie theatre?"
Kageaki"That too can be done."
Hikari"Amazing..."
Kageaki"Yes. But—"
Kageaki"If we don't get along, if we keep fighting, not only do we fail to build those things. Sometimes we destroy them also."
Hikari"That's bad..."
Kageaki"Yes."
Hikari"Then how do we stop fighting and get along?"
Kageaki"..."

Kageaki"The way you did, before."
Hikari"...?"
Kageaki"You gave someone your own food. Because you thought he was having more difficulty than you."
Kageaki"...It sounds a small thing. Doing it is not small. When they have enough for themselves, many people can be kind to others. When they themselves are suffering, very few can still do it."
Kageaki"When things become difficult, people think only of protecting themselves. Sometimes they even take from others to save themselves... You did not do that."
Hikari"..."
Kageaki"What you did was a very fine thing."
Hikari"...Oh..."
